passages.t: The fifth trumpet: the Abyss opened
passages.happening:
The fifth angel blows his trumpet, and John sees “a star that had fallen from heaven to earth, and it was given the key to the pit of the Abyss” (verse 1). The star opens the pit. Smoke pours out “like the smoke of a great furnace”, and the sun and the air are darkened (verse 2).

Out of the smoke come locusts with power to sting like scorpions (verse 3). “They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any plant or tree, but only those who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads” (verse 4). They may not kill, only torment, for five months (verse 5).

Then John says something about those days: “In those days men will seek death and will not find it; they will long to die, but death will escape them” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The eagle at the end of chapter 8 warned of three woes. This is the first. The first four trumpets struck the world around people. These strike people themselves, and they come from below.

The Abyss, in Greek abussos, the bottomless deep, was pictured as a prison for evil spirits. In Luke's Gospel the demons beg Jesus not to send them there. In the Greek Old Testament the same word is used for ‘the deep’ in Genesis 1:2. Here it is opened, and what comes out is darkness and torment.

But notice how often the passage says ‘given’ and ‘told’. The star is given the key. The locusts are given power. They are told what they may not touch. Evil is real, but it is neither free nor final. It acts only within the limits God sets.

And notice who is kept. The locusts may not touch those who have ‘the seal of God on their foreheads’. These are the servants sealed in chapter 7. The picture assures the churches that God's people belong to him even in the darkest scenes of the book.

Real locusts eat plants. These are forbidden to touch plants, and may attack only people. A locust lives for a season of several months, and some interpreters connect that with the ‘five months’. The number is a measure of scale and limit: the torment is real, but it has an end.
passages.ot:
The locusts come from Egypt's eighth plague: “The locusts swarmed across the land and settled over the entire territory of Egypt” and “Nothing green was left on any tree or plant in all the land of Egypt” (Exodus 10:14-15). Here, strangely, the plants are spared.

They come too from the prophet Joel, who described a real locust plague as an invading army. “Before them the earth quakes; the heavens tremble. The sun and moon grow dark, and the stars lose their brightness” (Joel 2:10).

And the deep is the deep of creation: “darkness was over the surface of the deep” (Genesis 1:2).
passages.hard:
‘Men will seek death and will not find it; they will long to die.’ How should a reader take a verse like this?

The verse describes people under judgment who are in such torment that they wish they were dead. It is a picture of misery, set in a vision. It does not say that wanting to die is right, and it gives no one permission to seek death. The whole book points the other way: God will wipe away every tear, and ‘there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain’ (21:4).

If this verse sounds like your own nights, please do not carry that alone. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that even the forces of the Abyss act only with a key they are given. Ask what it would mean to know that you are sealed as God's, even in dark days. And ask who around you might be in a darkness like this verse describes, and how you could stand with them.

passages.t: The locust army and its king
passages.happening:
John describes the locusts as best he can, and almost every line begins with ‘like’. They “looked like horses prepared for battle, with something like crowns of gold on their heads, and faces like the faces of men” (verse 7). “They had hair like that of women, and teeth like those of lions” (verse 8). They have breastplates like iron, and their wings sound “like the roar of many horses and chariots rushing into battle” (verse 9). Their tails sting like scorpions, with power to hurt people for five months (verse 10).

They have a king: “They were ruled by a king, the angel of the Abyss. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek it is Apollyon” (verse 11).

“The first woe has passed. Behold, two woes are still to follow” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
John keeps saying ‘like’. He is describing a vision in the language of comparison, not giving a report on real animals. The pictures are piled up to frighten the comfortable and the proud: horses, crowns, human faces, women's hair, lions' teeth, iron, the roar of chariots, scorpions' stings. It is an army of nightmare.

The king's two names tell us what he is. Abaddon is a Hebrew word meaning destruction. In the Old Testament it is used for the realm of the dead, alongside Sheol. Apollyon is Greek for destroyer. The king of the locusts is named by what he does. His rule is destruction. That stands in plain contrast to the God who creates and the Lamb who gives life. Some interpreters suspect a jab at the god Apollo, whose signs included the locust and whom some emperors claimed as a patron, but the link is uncertain.

The evils that fall on people in this chapter come from the Abyss, led by Destruction itself. Many interpreters see here a pattern found elsewhere in the Bible: God judges by handing people over to what they have chosen to serve. Paul says it in Romans 1: ‘God gave them over’.
passages.ot:
The lion's teeth and the noise of chariots are Joel's: “its teeth are the teeth of a lion” (Joel 1:6). “Their appearance is like that of horses, and they gallop like swift steeds. With a sound like that of chariots they bound over the mountaintops” (Joel 2:4-5).

Abaddon is the name of the realm of the dead in Job and Proverbs: “Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering” (Job 26:6), and “Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD” (Proverbs 15:11). Even the place of destruction is open before God.
passages.asks: Ask what the things people serve in place of God end up doing to them. Ask what it means that the enemy of God's people is named ‘Destroyer’, and the Lamb is the one who gives life. And ask whether you have seen in your own life what happens when you are handed over to what you chose.

passages.t: The sixth trumpet: the river Euphrates
passages.happening:
The sixth angel blows his trumpet, and John hears a voice “from the four horns of the golden altar before God” (verse 13). It says to the sixth angel, “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates” (verse 14).

The four angels, “who had been prepared for this hour and day and month and year”, are set free “to kill a third of mankind” (verse 15). John hears the number of the riders: two hundred million (verse 16).

Then he sees them: “The riders had breastplates the colors of fire, sapphire, and sulfur. The heads of the horses were like the heads of lions, and out of their mouths proceeded fire, smoke, and sulfur” (verse 17). A third of mankind is killed by the fire, smoke and sulfur (verse 18). The horses' power is in their mouths and in their tails, which are “like snakes, having heads with which to inflict harm” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The voice comes from the golden altar, the altar where the prayers of the saints rose with the incense in chapter 8. The judgments of this chapter are still part of God's answer to his people's cry for justice.

The Euphrates was the great river of the ancient Near East. In God's promise to Abraham it marked the far edge of the land. Across it came Israel's great oppressors, Assyria and Babylon, and Isaiah pictured the Assyrian army as the flood of that river. In John's day the Euphrates was the eastern border of the Roman empire. Beyond it lay Parthia, whose archers on horseback were famous for turning in the saddle to shoot behind them. A cavalry from the Euphrates whose horses harm with their tails would have stirred the dread of invasion from the east for readers in Asia.

The angels are held ready for ‘this hour and day and month and year’. Nothing happens by chance or before its time.

The numbers are huge: a third of mankind, two hundred million riders. They are best read as pictures of scale and limit. The harm is vast, and it is still partial.
passages.ot:
The Euphrates as the edge of the promise is from Genesis: “To your descendants I have given this land—from the river of Egypt to the great River Euphrates” (Genesis 15:18).

And the army from beyond it is Isaiah's picture: “the Lord will surely bring against them the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates— the king of Assyria and all his pomp” (Isaiah 8:7).
passages.hard:
What kind of God sends plagues that torment people and kill a third of mankind? And does this describe a war of our own time?

This is one of the hardest passages in the book, and a thoughtful reader will ask it sharply. A few things help, though they do not remove the weight. The picture is symbolic, and its numbers say that God's judgments in history are real and severe but limited, not that a count of the dead is being forecast. The destroyers come from the Abyss and from beyond the border: the evils that fall on idolatrous people are the forces they have chosen to serve, turned loose. And the purpose is repentance. The chapter's last word is sorrow that people did not turn, and the book keeps inviting even its enemies to fear God and give him glory (14:6-7).

Christians read the passage in the four ways the book page sets out, and these notes do not choose. Preterists tie it to fears of the first century and the armies of the Jewish war. Historicists in earlier centuries often matched the locusts and the riders with later invasions of the Christian world. Futurists expect real events in a final period. Idealists read it as a portrait of the self-destroying forces that idolatry sets loose in every age.

These notes tie no army, river, nation or war of our own day to this passage. Such matches have been made, and they have passed.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what borders you trust to keep danger out, and what it means that God holds even the hour and the day. Ask how you hold the weight of a passage like this without either smoothing it away or using it to frighten others. And ask what you would say to someone who reads this chapter and is afraid.

passages.happening:
John sees what the survivors do: “Now the rest of mankind who were not killed by these plagues still did not repent of the works of their hands. They did not stop worshiping demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk” (verse 20).

“Furthermore, they did not repent of their murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, and theft” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The chapter does not end with a victory. It ends with a sad verdict on the human heart. Even such judgments do not turn people from their idols.

The Greek word for repent, metanoeō, means to change one's mind and turn one's life around. Revelation uses it often. Christ called five of the seven churches to repent. Four times the book says that the nations would not. Repentance is always offered, and it is always a choice.

Notice what comes first in the list: idols. Revelation treats idolatry as the root of the other sins. The idols are made of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood, and they ‘cannot see or hear or walk’. People cling to lifeless gods even while they suffer what those gods bring.

Then come murder, sorcery, sexual sin and theft. The list broadly follows the order of the Ten Commandments: first false worship, then the sins against neighbours. ‘Sorcery’ translates the Greek pharmakeia, the use of drugs and spells in magic.

The chapter teaches a hard lesson. Suffering alone does not change a heart. Paul says that it is God's kindness that leads to repentance. The next two chapters turn from plagues to something else: the witness of God's people.
passages.ot:
The idols that cannot see or hear or walk are the psalm's: “Their idols are silver and gold, made by the hands of men. They have mouths, but cannot speak; they have eyes, but cannot see” (Psalm 115:4-5), and “they have feet, but cannot walk” (Psalm 115:7).

Daniel said the same to King Belshazzar, who “praised your gods of silver and gold, bronze and iron, wood and stone, which cannot see or hear or understand” (Daniel 5:23).
passages.hard:
If people will not repent even under judgment, what does change a human heart?

The chapter does not answer that question, but the whole New Testament does. Paul asks, “do you disregard the riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience, not realizing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?” (Romans 2:4). In Revelation, the next chapters show God's people bearing witness, and in 11:13 some do give glory to God.

And the same Christ who warned the churches also stands at the door and knocks (3:20). The door of repentance stays open in this book far longer than its plagues might suggest.
passages.asks: Ask what people today keep trusting even when it keeps failing them. Ask what, in your own life, has actually changed your heart: suffering, or kindness, or both. And ask what idol you would find hardest to give up, even if it cost you.
